items.body:
### Proposal Details

This proposal suggests adding support for `RFC 9557` Internet Extended Date/Time Format (IXDTF) to Go's `time` package. IXDTF is a backward-compatible extension of RFC 3339 that adds optional suffix elements for timezone names and metadata.

https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9557.html

## Background

RFC 9557, published in 2024, extends RFC 3339 by allowing additional suffix information while maintaining full backward compatibility. This enables more precise time representation for internationalization, calendar systems, and metadata preservation.

### Current State
`time` package has excellent RFC 3339 support with optimized parsing and formatting functions (`parseRFC3339`, `appendFormatRFC3339`). However, it cannot handle IXDTF's extended format.

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/time/format_rfc3339.go

### Examples

```
Basic RFC 3339:
2006-01-02T15:04:05Z
2006-01-02T15:04:05.999999999-07:00

IXDTF with timezone:
2006-01-02T15:04:05Z[UTC]
2006-01-02T15:04:05+09:00[Asia/Tokyo]

IXDTF with extensions:
2006-01-02T15:04:05Z[u-ca=japanese]
2006-01-02T15:04:05+09:00[Asia/Tokyo][u-ca=japanese]

IXDTF with critical extensions:
2006-01-02T15:04:05Z[!u-ca=japanese]
```

## Motivation

1. **Standards Compliance**: RFC 9557 is an official IETF standard extending RFC 3339
2. **Internationalization**: Better support for non-Gregorian calendars and localization
3. **Interoperability**: Compatibility with systems already using IXDTF
4. **Metadata Preservation**: Ability to preserve timezone and calendar information in serialization

## Proposed API (Initial Concept)

```go
// New constants
const (
    RFC9557TimeZone     = "2006-01-02T15:04:05Z07:00[time-zone]"
    RFC9557NanoTimeZone = "2006-01-02T15:04:05.999999999Z07:00[time-zone]"
)

// Extension information structure
type IXDTFExtensions struct {
    TimeZone  string            // IANA timezone name
    Tags      map[string]string // Extension tags
    Critical  map[string]bool   // Critical flags
}

// New parsing/formatting functions
func (t Time) appendFormatRFC9557(b []byte, nanos bool, ext IXDTFExtensions) []byte
func parseRFC9557[bytes []byte | string](s bytes, local *Location) (Time, IXDTFExtensions, bool)
```

items.body:
### Proposal Details

To help building dev tools which are `go tool`-aware, especially with a separate `go.mod` dedicated to manage tools dependencies (ex: `go tool -modfile=tools.mod`), I propose to extend `go tool` to propagate its `-modfile` flag value to the child processes via an environment variable:
* When `go tool` runs with `-modfile`, expose the flag value as variable `GOTOOLMOD` (similar to the existing `GOMOD`) when running (NOT building) the tool
* When `go tool` runs without `-modfile`, use the value of `GOTOOLMOD` environment variable, if available, as the first fallback value for locating the `go.mod` to use for resolving (and building) tools binaries. If building a tool is necessary, clear `GOTOOLMOD` from the environment before calling `go build`. Keep `GOTOOLMOD` in the environment when executing the tool.


## Use cases

### `go tool` called from a tool

A tool called via `go tool` might want to call another tool, also via `go tool`.

A tool called via `go tool -modfile=tools.mod` might want to call another tool, also via `go tool`, but with the same `go.mod` file. For that case, the default value for `-modfile` for `go tool` would be set from the `GOTOOLMOD` value. The first tool would just execute `go tool` and would not have to specially care about `-modfile`.

Example: a `go generate` command that calls a tool local to the module which then calls an external tool.

### A tool that manages tools

A tool that manages tools need to be aware that it is called via `go tool` (see #78673) but also which `go.mod` to use/tweak. While it could have its own `-modfile` flag, it would be simpler to make it aware implicitly of the `go.mod` via an environment variable `GOTOOLMOD`.

## Related proposals

* complementary to #78673: a wider proposal about exposing _some_ environment variable(s) that allow a tool to be aware of being launched via `go tool`

### Proposal Details

## Summary

`go tool` set environment variable(s) that allows a tool to identify being run from `go tool`.

## Proposal

When `go tool` executes a tool, set the following variables:
* `GOTOOL=<tool import path>`
* `GOTOOLMOD=<go.mod used by "go tool -modfile">` to allow recursive call to `go tool` with another tool from the same go.mod (details in #79449 )
* `GOTOOLVERSION=<module version of the tool>` if not the main module (see also #75033 which is about [`runtime/debug.BuildInfo`](https://pkg.go.dev/runtime/debug#BuildInfo) for tools)

As a tool being called by `go tool` might itself call another tool via `go tool`, all `go tool` specific environment variables of a parent tool execution must be overwritten or deleted.

## Rationale

Tools can currently run in two modes:
* _stand-alone_: when installed with `go install <tool>@<version>` and executed as normal commands from the shell
* _module tool_: when declared in go.mod and executed through `go tool <tool>`

To improve integration of tools with the Go toolchain, I think that tools should be able to distinguish in which mode they are being executed: when running _stand-alone_, they should be able to detect if they are working in a Go module which has declared them, and then work just as a shim that delegate to `go tool` to the specific version selected for the project is executed.

The purpose of this proposal is to help the tool to distinguish if it is being executed via `go tool` (_stand-alone_ vs _module tool_ as defined above).

For example `golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer` installed with `go install` should be able to detect that it is executed from a Go module that has `golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer` declared (and so locked to a specific version), and then forward its arguments to `go tool golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stringer`. But to avoid infinite recursion, `stringer` should be able to discover if it is already running via `go tool`.

items.title: proposal: Go: add a zero-value test operator

labels.name: LanguageChange
labels.description: Suggested changes to the Go language

labels.name: LanguageChangeReview
labels.description: Discussed by language change review committee

milestone.title: Proposal
milestone.description:
Proposals that are pending (not yet accepted/rejected).
See https://go.dev/s/proposal-process.

items.body:
Add unary `~` for testing whether a value is non-zero. `!~x` tests whether it is zero.

```go
if ~err {}          // err != nil
if ~ptr {}          // ptr != nil
if ~iface {}        // iface != nil

if ~slice {}        // slice != nil
if ~dict {}         // dict != nil
if ~ch {}           // ch != nil
if ~fn {}           // fn != nil

if ~str {}          // str != ""
if ~n {}            // n != 0
if ~f {}            // f != 0.0; +0.0 and -0.0 are both zero

if ~len(slice) {}   // len(slice) != 0
if ~len(dict) {}    // len(dict) != 0
if ~len(ch) {}      // len(ch) != 0
if ~len(str) {}     // len(str) != 0

if !~x {}           // x is zero
```

Structs and arrays are tested recursively:

```go
type Config struct {
    Name    string
    Tags    []string
    Headers map[string]string
}

var cfg Config

if ~cfg {} // false

cfg.Name = "server"
if ~cfg {} // true

cfg = Config{Tags: []string{}}
if ~cfg {} // true
```

This also works for structs containing non-comparable fields, where ordinary equality cannot be used.

For reference-like values, zero means `nil`, not empty:

```go
var a []int
b := []int{}

if ~a {}       // false
if ~b {}       // true

if ~len(a) {}  // false
if ~len(b) {}  // false
```

## Generics

The operator is valid for any type, including unconstrained type parameters:

```go
func NonZero[T any](v T) bool {
    return ~v
}

func IsZero[T any](v T) bool {
    return !~v
}
```

This allows generic zero-value testing without requiring `T` to satisfy `comparable`.

For example:

```go
func FirstNonZero[T any](values ...T) T {
    for _, v := range values {
        if ~v {
            return v
        }
    }

    var zero T
    return zero
}
```

## Motivation

Go frequently tests values against zero using different expressions such as:

```go
err != nil
name != ""
count != 0
len(items) != 0
```

`~` provides one concise and uniform zero-value test across all Go types, including non-comparable structs and unconstrained generic types.

## Compatibility

This change is source-compatible with existing valid Go programs. Unary `~` currently has no value-expression meaning, so existing programs are unaffected.

```go
type unit = struct{}
```

```go
type any = interface{}
```

`struct{}` is widely used in Go when a type is required but no information needs to be stored, for example:

```go
map[string]struct{}
```

```go
map[string]unit

```

The name `unit` reflects the semantics of `struct{}`: it is a zero-size type with exactly one possible value. It also avoids the ambiguity of `void`, which commonly means the absence of a value in other languages.

items.title: proposal: cmd/go, x/mod: add test-scoped requirements in go.mod

labels.name: LanguageProposal
labels.description: Issues describing a requested change to the Go language specification.

milestone.title: Proposal
milestone.description:
Proposals that are pending (not yet accepted/rejected).
See https://go.dev/s/proposal-process.

items.body:
### Proposal Details

## Motivation

Go 1.24 introduced a first-class way to declare and run **developer tools** via the `tool` directive and `go get -tool`, removing the historic `tools.go` workaround. This neatly captures *executable* developer dependencies (linters, generators, etc.).  

However, there is still no first-class way to distinguish **test-only library dependencies** (e.g. `github.com/stretchr/testify`, `github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go`) from runtime requirements.

Today:

- Test-only deps appear in `require` like everything else after `go mod tidy`, because the module graph must be complete for `go test` and `go mod` operations.  
- Users often want the guarantee “my **final binary** only links the standard library (or at least: no packages from these test-only modules).” There’s no declarative way to express or enforce that intent in `go.mod`.

While Go’s linker already strips unused packages (so test deps are *not* linked into binaries), the inability to **declare** and **audit** that a dependency is *test-only* creates friction:

- Reviews can’t easily tell which requirements are runtime-critical vs test-only.  
- Vendoring, SBOMs, and compliance reports often over-report because the scope is implicit.  
- Tools and CI lack a simple switch to “fail the build if any non-stdlib runtime dependency sneaks in”.

---

## Prior art

- **Go 1.24 tool directive.** Tracks dev *tools* without polluting runtime deps.  
- **Community requests.** Similar asks to separate dev/test deps have surfaced before but were closed without syntax.  
- **Current behaviour.** `go mod tidy` includes what’s needed to run tests; test deps aren’t linked into the final binary, but they are indistinguishable in `go.mod`.  
- **General module semantics.** The reference manual describes `require`, `replace`, `exclude`, `retract`, and now `tool`, but has no test-scope.  

---

## Proposal

Introduce a **test scope** for requirements in `go.mod`.

### Syntax options

**A. Inline annotation** (least disruptive):

```go
module example.com/app

go 1.24

require (
    github.com/acme/runtime-lib v1.2.3
    github.com/stretchr/testify v1.9.0 // test
    github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go v0.31.1 // test
)
```

**B. Block form** (mirrors `tool`/`require` grouping):

```go
module example.com/app

go 1.24

require (
    github.com/acme/runtime-lib v1.2.3
)

testrequire (
    github.com/stretchr/testify v1.9.0
    github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go v0.31.1
)
```

---

### Semantics

- **Resolution:**  
  - `go test` treats test-scoped requirements as available like normal `require`.  
  - `go build` and `go install` ignore test-scoped requirements unless pulled in by `_test.go` or `testmain`.  

- **MVS & sums:**  
  - Test-scoped modules participate in MVS *only for test builds*.  
  - Checksums still live in `go.sum` as usual.

- **Tidy & vendor:**  
  - `go mod tidy` keeps test-scoped requirements only as needed for `go test ./...`.  
  - `go mod vendor` gains `-test` (default **on**) and `-notest` to include/omit test-scoped modules.

- **Listing & audit:**  
  - `go list -m -test all` includes test-scoped modules.  
  - `go list -m all` excludes them by default (or vice-versa, depending on Go team preference).  

- **Enforcement switch:**  
  - Add `-enforce=stdlib` to `go build` to fail if any non-stdlib packages are linked.  
  - Useful for teams that want “stdlib-only binaries”.

---

## Rationale

- **Clarity:** Makes intent explicit in the manifest.  
- **Reproducibility & policy:** Enables CI checks like “no runtime third-party deps”.  
- **Consistency:** Symmetric with Go 1.24’s `tool` directive (tools vs test libraries are distinct categories).

---

## Backward compatibility

- Existing modules remain valid.  
- Comments (`// test`) are ignored by old toolchains.  
- If the block form is chosen (`testrequire`), older toolchains will show “unknown directive” and proceed with only regular `require`s.  
- No change to package import semantics, build tags, or linking.

---

## Alternatives considered

1. **Status quo** (infer from `_test.go`): remains ambiguous in manifests, awkward for vendoring/SBOM.  
2. **Use `tool` for test libs:** incorrect, since `tool` targets *executable* tools and integrates with `go tool`, not packages.  
3. **Separate `tools.go` / build tags:** legacy workaround that Go 1.24 intentionally superseded for tools, and it doesn’t help for test libraries.  

---

## Examples

### go.mod

```go
module example.com/service

go 1.24

require (
    github.com/acme/runtime-lib v1.2.3
    github.com/stretchr/testify v1.9.0 // test
    github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go v0.31.1 // test
)
```

### Commands

```bash
# CI: ensure no non-stdlib packages are linked (optional complementary flag)
go build -enforce=stdlib ./cmd/service

# Vendor only runtime deps
go mod vendor -notest

# List only runtime module requirements
go list -m all

# List including test-scoped requirements
go list -m -test all
```

---

## Open questions

- **Exact syntax**: inline comment vs new block keyword. Inline is minimally invasive; a new block is more explicit and tool-friendly.  
- **Go vet / lint integration**: should `vet` warn if a test-scoped module is imported by non-test code?  
- **Workspace (`go.work`)**: should there be a way to apply test scope across multiple modules coherently?

---

items.title: proposal: cmd/go: allow multiple packages per directory

milestone.title: Proposal
milestone.description:
Proposals that are pending (not yet accepted/rejected).
See https://go.dev/s/proposal-process.

items.body:
### Background

Currently, the Go toolchain enforces that all .go source files within the same directory must declare the same package name, with the only exception being test files (_test.go), which may use <pkg> or <pkg>_test.
This constraint simplifies tooling, but often forces developers to create many small directories even when the code is logically related and naturally belongs together.

### Motivation

There are situations where allowing multiple packages in a single directory would improve project organization and developer productivity:

Testing patterns: today, the only way to test a package externally (mypkg_test) is by creating a special _test package. It would be more consistent if multiple packages could coexist more generally.

Domain separation: sometimes you want two closely related packages (e.g., domain and domain_testimpl) that share resources in the same directory tree. Forcing a new directory is artificial and bloats the project structure.

Reducing boilerplate: large projects end up with a very deep directory tree only because of this limitation, not because of actual modularity needs. This increases navigation cost and fragmentation.

### Proposal

Allow the Go toolchain to accept multiple packages within the same directory. Example:

```go
// file: repo/user.go
package repo
type UserRepo struct{}

// file: repo/user_mock.go
package repo_mock
type UserRepoMock struct{}
```

Both files would live in repo/, and go build ./repo/... would build both packages.

### Considerations

- Tooling impact: IDEs, go build, go list, go install, etc., would need to account for multiple packages per directory. Currently, go list ./repo assumes a single package. We would need to decide if it should return multiple entries.
- Clarity: today the rule “one directory = one package” is simple and easy to teach. Relaxing it adds flexibility, but also complexity.
- Migration: existing projects would not break, since they already conform. This is an opt-in feature.
- Tests: the _test package special case would become a natural extension of this feature, making Go’s package rules more consistent.

### Alternatives considered

- Keep current restriction and live with deep directory hierarchies.
- Use internal/ packages for separation, but this is heavier than necessary.
- Code generation or symlinks, which are workarounds, not clean solutions.

### Conclusion

Allowing multiple packages per directory would give developers more flexibility, reduce artificial directory nesting, and simplify certain testing and mocking scenarios. While it adds complexity to tooling, it aligns better with practical needs for large-scale projects.

items.body:
### Proposal Details

Recently, there have been more and more news like
https://socket.dev/blog/11-malicious-go-packages-distribute-obfuscated-remote-payloads
or
https://alexandear.github.io/posts/2025-02-28-malicious-go-programs/
etc
I propose to implement at the api level the ability to monitor and modify a variety of system calls.
Following the example of how it's already done in python
https://docs.python.org/3/library/audit_events.html
But it's done very poorly there, and it would be useful to implement a full-fledged hook subsystem like
```
audit.Handle(os.RemoveAll, func(path string) error {
    fmt.Println("Path remove request for:", path)
    switch path {
        case "/bin":
            return nil // deny
        case "/tmp/old":
            return os.Rename(path, "/tmp/new") // replace call
        case "/home":
            path = "/tmp/trash" // replace argument
    }
    return os.RemoveAll(path)
})
```
or
```
audit.Handle(http.Get, func(url string) (resp *http.Response, err error) {
    fmt.Println("Http get request for:", url)
    switch url {
        case "some.malware.host":
            return nil, nil
        default:
            url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080"
    }
    return http.Get(url)
})
```
All this can be done anyway if start inject handler code directly in the golang source code, but why spoil it if you can add a separate powerful subsystem.

### Proposal Details

<details>

<summary>Filled out language-change form, collapsed</summary>

**Would you consider yourself a novice, intermediate, or experienced Go programmer?**

Experienced.

**What other languages do you have experience with?**

Numerous; relevantly here, Haskell, Typescript, a wide suite of dynamically-typed languages.

**Would this change make Go easier or harder to learn, and why?**

Minimally harder.

**Has this idea, or one like it, been proposed before? If so, how does this proposal differ?**

Several sum type proposals. I have read them all. This one differs in that rather than being a brand new feature it is a minor extension of an existing one.

**Who does this proposal help, and why?**

It does provide a blessed and cleaned-up mechanism for handling situations in the expression problem when some particular bit of code needs to focus on adding operations in external packages.

**What is the proposed change? Please describe as precisely as possible the change to the language. What would change in the language spec? Please also describe the change informally, as in a class teaching Go.**

See all that below.

**Is this change backward compatible? Breaking the Go 1 compatibility guarantee is a large cost and requires a large benefit.**

Yes.

**Show example code before and after the change.**

See below.

**What is the cost of this proposal? (Every language change has a cost).**

Fairly minimal.

**How many tools (such as vet, gopls, gofmt, goimports, etc.) would be affected?**

There would be some sort of new keyword that would need to be added or some other syntax change. However it is nearly identical to existing constructs; many such tools could just alias the new keyword as a new spelling of `interface` and continue providing the same services as before.

**What is the compile time cost?**

Verifying that an embedding chain (to coin a term) doesn't terminate in a sum-type interface is a negligible cost.

**What is the run time cost?**

Already paid in existing techniques.

**Can you describe a possible implementation?**

See below.

**Do you have a prototype? (This is not required.) How would the language spec change? Orthogonality: how does this change interact or overlap with existing features?**

See below.

**Is the goal of this change a performance improvement? Does this affect error handling? Is this about generics?**

No, no, and no.

</details>

# Overview

In my opinion, a lot of sum type discussion on the internet (not necessarily any given proposal here) has taken it as read that in order to have "sum types", they must look and act exactly as they do in other languages, or they aren't "real" sum types.

But I think far more important is to look at sum types, look at how they are used, extract from them the capabilities we are looking for, then look at how we put those capabilities in Go in the most harmonious manner, rather than potentially introducing long-term warts into Go.

The capabilities one might want from a sum type:

* A set of typed product values that can be used as a single type in a type declaration.
* This set is closed; external packages can not add to it.
* Since it is closed, exhaustiveness checking is possible, whether in a compiler or a linter like `go vet`.
* The ability to do some sort of type switch on the components of the sum type.
* Compiler optimization to take advantage of the closed nature of the type to pack it more efficiently in RAM is at least possible.

  I don't intend that as part of this proposal, but I think this can be used as a metric for measuring it; it should be _possible_ for a compiler to implement this based on the proposal, even though I would not consider implementing that as part of this proposal. I believe this is the case but if anyone can show otherwise I would consider that a substantial criticism.

Thus, the correct question is not "how can we _transliterate_ sum types into Go?" but "how can we _translate_ the features sum types provide into Go?"

It is well-known that you can get close to meeting all of the above criteria in current Go simply by declaring an unexported method in an interface:

```
type MySumType interface {
    Name() string
    isMySumType()
}

type Red struct {}
func (r Red) isMySumType() {}
func (r Red) Name() string { return "red" }

func DoSomething(val MySumType) {
    switch v := val.(type) {
    case Red:
        // etc.
    }
}

```

But this does not quite get there, because there is a hole in the system, plenty large enough to ruin these use cases in practice. A struct in an external package can embed the interface representing the sum type. This struct then automatically conforms to the interface. This causes two problems:

1. Instances of this new struct can be passed to `DoSomething`, but it is impossible for the type switch to match it and do anything useful with it. So `DoSomething` can't count on the guarantee of receiving only a bounded set of types known at the time it was written.
2. This struct can also override any exported methods, which means those aren't available for the sum type to make any guarantees about, as the overriding implementation can break those guarantees with impunity. This may be somewhat less Go-like, but it is very similar to the desire to know the function can receive only a constrained set of types, and in particular the constrained methods that would be on those types.

See [this example](https://go.dev/play/p/DohbnLxFWMY) on the Go Playground for concrete code.

If it weren't for this particular issue, this would largely, and I believe entirely, meet the criteria above.

# Proposal

Therefore, my proposal is that rather than trying to build a complicated new feature, we simply fix the problem that embedding interface types creates. Allow an interface to declare that it can't be embedded by a struct, which we can call `sum_interface`:

```
package somepackage

type MySumType sum_interface {
    Name() string
    isMySumType()
}

// Red and other elements of MySumType as above
```

It would then be a compiler error for an **external** package to embed this interface value into a struct, by any amount of embedding recursion or type aliasing. The package that offers the `sum_interface` can do it, because any code that switches on the types could account for its own internal type, but external packages would be forbidden to embed it.

It is not necessary to block embedding into an interface. All an external interface declaration can do is further narrow the interface, if the sum type-providing package exports the parts of the sum types and if those types have methods that may allow further distinguishing of the components. Type assertion can be used like normal to test if a member of a sum interface is or is not also a member of some narrowed interface.

A `sum_interface` must include a non-exported method or the compiler should error. The compiler imposes no constraints beyond "some unexported method". I'm using verbose `isThisType()` methods as an example, but any unexported method will do. As a matter of style rather than requirement, if there is a sensible method to put on the `sum_interface` that perform some actual task, so much the better. Empty tag methods are only required when there is no useful method otherwise. In the event this proposal was to be accepted I would advise documentation to treat tagging with a useful method as the primary case, and mention in the prose that you can create a do-nothing "tag" method as well, lest people think that the tag methods are mandatory because that's what the docs show.

I am not passionate about this syntax, though I would observe I don't think `type MySumType sum interface` is a good idea since that makes it look like there could be other modifiers. I weakly recommend some single token, and recommend against a pragma. This is the most bikesheddable portion of this entire proposal and I doubt anything I can put here will prevent it from happening anyhow, so I will deliberately harness it instead of fighting it.

## Interface Semantics Retained

A type can implement multiple sum type interfaces at once, because it can implement multiple interfaces at once and there is no reason to exclude this possibility. This differs from most sum types in most languages, but I personally do not consider this a requirement for sum types. I see no reason why it is _mandatory_ for the individual components of a sum type to be fully disjoint at the type level from the components of other sum types. There may be pros and cons to each possibility, and other languages may build further structure on top of the choice they make, but I do not see it as integral to the concept, nor do I see it as integral that it _must_ be impossible to use the type system to specify just some particular component of the sum type.

This requires no additional semantic specifications beyond it being a compile error to embed an unembedable interface, as interfaces are already fully specified in Go. For instance, it is obvious how this works with generic interfaces, because a "generic sum type" _is_ just a generic interface, including usage in constraints: It works exactly as it would today without the `sum_interface` annotation.  It is also clear how to use a sum interface as a generic constraint, for the same reason. Further it should be future-proof; any future work on interfaces should automatically apply to sum types and extend them appropriately.

I would personally propose leaving exhaustiveness checking to external linters that interested users can easily integrate into their compilation process and in most cases directly into their development environment. This prevents the Go project itself from having to take a stance on whether a "complete" type switch includes `nil` or not, which is situational. This is also fairly bikesheddable, although in this case I think the divergences in opinions are fundamental, and that shifting them out into a linter is not just punting, but actually the correct decision for Go.

## `reflect` Implications

`reflect.StructOf` should panic if a user attempts to embed a `sum_interface` as an anonymous field. As it stands now [it looks like this is already implemented because `StructOf` already panics on attempts to embed an interface with unexported methods](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.26.4:src/reflect/type.go;l=2397), which references [a 2016 issue #15924](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/15924). Implementing this proposal complicates ever fixing that issue, though it shouldn't make it impossible. 

I can't find a reason this would need to be a separate `reflect.Kind`. I can't even find a concrete reason at the moment that a method to indicate something like `CanEmbedInStruct() bool` would need to be added. The utility of such a method to prevent panics from misusing `reflect.StructOf` is apparently already not enough to make it worth including in the `reflect` package today.

I did a [search for reflect.StructOf](https://github.com/search?q=language%3Ago+reflect.StructOf&type=code) on GitHub and it turned up 167 distinct uses as of my search. (It initially says many thousands but if you click through it dedupes and consolidates and the number drops dramatically.) Perusing those it seems to be mostly cases like constructing structs for use with reflect-based serializers, database interaction, and other cases where it doesn't seem likely that the users have any use for an anonymous field, especially since it is currently impossible to embed an interface with an unexported field into a struct anyhow.

I would also observe that any sum type proposal that involves adding a new `reflect.Kind` is arguably a violation of the Go 1.0 compatibility promise. Introducing a new `reflect.Kind` into the set of possibilities could break a lot of code.

# Standard Library Prior Art

There is an example of this in the standard library, modulo the use of the `sum_interface` type to enforce it.

The [standard library `ast` package]((https://pkg.go.dev/go/ast)) nearly implements this proposal. It has four disjoint sum types, [`Expr`, `Stmt`, `Decl`](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.26.4:src/go/ast/ast.go;l=42), and [Spec](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.26.4:src/go/ast/ast.go;l=903), each with a corresponding `exprNode()` or similar unexported method.

It turns out they also provide a standard-library example of the utility of the ability to build on these using the standard Go tools for interfaces. The [`Node` type](https://pkg.go.dev/go/ast#Node) is an interface that also joins all the AST node types into one unifying type. This type includes all the types that implement `Expr`, `Stmt`, etc., directly, without creating a wrapper type for `Expr` that has to be deconstructed itself. `Node` technically is not a sum type, as it has only exported methods, but it incorporates all the node types in the previous paragraph. But a function like [`Unparen`](https://pkg.go.dev/go/ast#Unparen) nails down the argument it takes to just the `Expr` type, which if you consider `Node` as a _de facto_ sum type demonstrates composing together multiple sum types, and/or narrowing broad sum types, already in the standard library. `Node` also includes types that aren't any of those four things. Not all languages that implement sum types have an analog to this flexibility.

(If an external package tries to create new types that implements `Node`, while it is technically possible, it's walking into a minefield, because of things like the [Walk function panicking on unknown `Node` members](https://cs.opensource.google/go/go/+/refs/tags/go1.26.4:src/go/ast/walk.go;l=351).  I think it's reasonable for me to cite this as an example of four sum types that are then composed cleanly into one overarching sum type, even if `Node` does not contain an unexported method.)

# Weakness

## Sum Types Always Have A `nil`

Sum types in this proposal always end up with `nil` as a valid value and there is no type-based way to get rid of that.

I have seen at least one other sum type proposal some work on trying to figure out how to define a "zero value" for the sum type to avoid this. I believe this should be treated orthogonally to the question of sum types in general. If it is desirable to work out how to avoid a `nil` getting forcibly adjoined to sum types by creating some sort of declaration of what a "zero value" is for the type, it is equally desirable for the several other types that have the same problem. A "solution" to that problem that works only for sum types only makes the foreignness of such a solution to the rest of Go even worse. E.g., people declaring a "sum type" with only one component type like an int so that they can get a default value of "100" just to get the defaulting behavior would be quite the wart.

If it is desirable to solve this problem it should be solved for Go as a whole, not just for sum types.

As it stands for the purposes of this proposal, a `nil` is a perfectly normal thing in Go and it is well beyond the scope of this proposal to try to change something so fundamental.

## Sum Types Have Methods

A lot of people associate sum types with functional programming, which tends to eschew methods. Some critics may claim that sum types that have methods aren't "real sum types".

However, both Zig and Nim have sum types that can have methods defined on them. Given that their sum types can also be of types that have methods on them themselves, they even have the equivalent of the ability to assert some aspect of the sum type is of some type that can have methods called on it, and then call methods on it.

One could argue this puts Go closer to the cutting edge in what sum types are doing in the latest languages, rather than necessarily being "wrong".

It's hard to know every language. An AI search suggests that there may not be any other major languages that allow methods on their official sum type implementation anyhow, suggesting that the behavior of methods on sum types is not something the community at large has strong opinions about yet.

## Methods Can't Change The Underlying Type

However, one thing Zig's and Nim's methods can do that Go would not under this proposal is [have a method on a sum type change the "branch" the sum type is in](https://codapi.org/embed/?sandbox=zig&code=data%3A%3Bbase64%2CfZDNaoQwFIX3PsXBlQ4SmZ8Wqgh9h5auCkPUWEP1ZjAxwyBuu%2B4z9klKokMZWppdcu93Ts6pFGkDbWoUeJT9SQ0mCrWpwzgPgsoPX3iHAiNJRZGgsY8xBQAgyWSQ%2B13ib02nuMnQ3B%2BSwD8s8JPoGif93EodxTmANMXXxydMKzWkhmkF3sUFnSSxgKexREPQwhyNOnrdSIuuybBxagmst4lhlazXv7jjdtgGBdgE5jEUsJhX0340vOwu0GdpqlZolAOnqvX4%2FJezpN%2B%2Bcr%2F731fS1XUVnvMgWHV7Lim6wS0fnOrS8A9%2B2F15y25q2LPtYXv3EC%2FDNIV1FZI632Ret66ptKlZLcrxjZ0GlymcOF3mVwoTsMnOcR7M3w%3D%3D). The linked example shows a Zig union of an `int32` and a `float64` (in Go type terms) and shows methods that mutate a value of that type populated by one of the constituent types and flip it to the other type.

Go would not be able to do this. No method declared in the sum interface can mutate to another type because no method can mutate the concrete type of what it is called on. Since this proposal doesn't propose to tie types to belong to specific sum interfaces, and specific types may participate in more than one of them, the implementation of a method couldn't know what other types would be valid, a necessary prerequisite to any "solution" to this.

A function could implement this behavior by taking a pointer to the sum interface value. Taking a pointer to an interface is generally considered "weird" in Go. I think it would continue to be so. This seems like an edge case most people aren't interested in as sum types are generally associated with a style of programming that would just return a new value instead. I think this provides good enough coverage of what is already an edge-case that there's no need to try to cover this use case in the main proposal.

## Interface Unmarshaling

An interface-based sum type inherits the problems with the common reflect-based approaches to unmarshaling into interface values; that is not new. What is new to this proposal is that it also blocks the solution I most commonly deploy for that, which is to embed the interface directly into a struct:

```
type MarshalableSumType struct {
    sumtypepkg.MySumType
}
```

and then implement marshaling methods on it, while the interface is transparently proxied to the embedded value by struct embedding's semantics.

The package that implements sum types could offer a marshaling struct like that, because a package is allowed to embed its own sum type. That essentially makes the `MarshalableSumType` a new member of the sum type that all code within the package now must deal with, which is slighty tedious but possible. This would permit a fixed set of marshalers to be defined by a package offering a sum interface type. But there would still be no way to directly embed the type as above, and so packages would have no ability to add their own marshaling that the original package may not have known about. Such a package would have to declare a struct with a named member.

Reflect-based marshaling is already only a convenient shortcut even at the best of times anyhow. There are many use cases where it breaks down and something more manual has to be implemented. If this proposal added the first thing that broke the utility of standard reflect-based marshaling, that would be a big strike against it, but it joins an already substantial list and I don't think it's a qualitative change. It is already common to have to fall back to other approaches for pieces of a marshaling process.

## All Sum Type Values Will Get Boxed Initially

As I mentioned towards the beginning, if this proposal has succeeded in its goals, it should be safe for the compiler to implement optimizations to pack a value of this interface in a way that is more efficient and unboxed in practice. 

However were this to be accepted I wouldn't expect this to be immediately implemented, so there will be a phase where all sum types would be boxed and quite likely difficult to prevent from going to the heap.

Then again that is already the case for the large amounts of code implementing sum types this way, just without the embedding guarantees provided by this proposal.

If this is a big concern it should be fixable in the future without any changes to the specification.

## No Pattern Matching

Some people think pattern matching goes with sum types. I think it's orthogonal, in that you can have pattern matching without them and sum types with no pattern matching.

Go has the most useful kind already, which is the top-level type switch using `switch val.(type)`. I believe anything further would be a separate spec. Pattern matching should work with non-sum types anyhow.

## This Won't Silence The Critics

Most of the people complaining that Go doesn't have sum types will probably not accept this as a sum type, because it doesn't look the way they expect. Especially due to the fact that the branches of the sum type continue to be specified as they are today, without any sort of syntax gloss on trying to "bundle" them together. Some of the other sum type proposals have attempted to sketch these out but I don't believe I've seen one that I would even call "good", let alone worthy of inclusion in the language specification. I wasn't able to come up with anything better in my own exploration of this proposal.

I suspect the intersection of "people who already or may someday use Go" and the very loudest of these critics is not all that large anyhow, and having a blessed mechanism will satisfy most of the Go users who have wanted a sum type.

But I think it is fair to observe that this proposal will shift those critics from "Go is lacking sum types" to "Go's sum types are weird and wrong" rather than "Go finally has sum types!". Although as I will address at the end, I'm not convinced there is any sum type proposal that Go can integrate that will not have this problem anyhow.

# Conclusion

Cards on the table, I will admit to some bias here. I believe that in Go as it is constituted today, it is almost always the correct software engineering choice to [replace conditional with polymorphism](https://refactoring.guru/replace-conditional-with-polymorphism). I believe that the vast majority of things that people think are "sum types", if you apply this principle consistently to them, end up putting everything into methods and dissolve away the entire need to switch on the type, and in many cases, also dissolve away the utility of closing the interface as well. I believe my awareness of this technique is why I don't miss them in Go very often.

However, I agree that there are rare, but definitely existing, cases where that is not a viable answer, because there are times when one absolutely, positively _needs_ the ability to add operations to a type in external packages. AST nodes are a classic case, perhaps the canonical case of this, but it isn't the only case.

There is no need to try to yank Go all the way from the side of the [expression problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expression_problem) it is currently on to the other. We can acknowledge that the need to add operations to existing types is the less usual case in a language that prioritizes adding additional types to existing operations when possible, and simply clean up/make possible handling the other side without trying to completely conquer both sides, which few, and arguably no, languages have ever done.

Other than the fact this doesn't "look like" sum types when read off the screen, and the IMHO orthogonal issue of the zero value always being included in a sum type, this:

* Covers all the bases of _functionality_ that people are looking for.
* Resolves the tension of sum types having substantial and complicated overlapping with interfaces by simply being a simple extension of interfaces.
* Minimizes the impact on the language, both in terms of analyzing this against the current language and minimizing reducing the options on any future capabilities.
* Makes it possible to do some things with "sum types" most other languages don't support, such as mixing and matching the types that implement various `sum` interfaces in a package as `ast` already does.
* Minimizes the difficulty of implementation and the probability of any other surprises discovered in the implementation.
* Breaks apart the need to nail down functionality and syntax in one proposal; future proposals can argue about how to syntax-sugar this without blocking functionality, most likely never happening.

So while this may result in a "sum type" that doesn't much _look_ like sum types in other languages, there is the compensation that they have some additional capabilities not normally associated with sum types, plus the fact that it plays with existing Go tools and future Go tools probably better than any other proposal could.

Philosophically, I think one of the reasons it has been so difficult to figure out how to put a sum type implementation into Go is that the overlap with `interface` isn't superficial. It is quite substantial. A "closed interface" today gets you 90% of the way there, and I think there's something fundamentally and profoundly true about that. I think a solid argument can be made that no other conceivable proposal for "sum types" can ever be made to work without all but breaking Go as a coherent language because the overlap is too large and there simply isn't _room_ for any other concept of sum types in Go. I'll cop to some vigorous handwaving on that point, but I think previous conversations in the previous issues can only be seen as evidence in favor of this claim.

items.body:
### Proposal Details

## Abstract

This proposal adds associated types to named Go interfaces. An associated type is determined by an implementing type rather than chosen independently by each generic function.

```go
type Container interface {
	type Element any
	Add(Element)
	At(int) (Element, bool)
}

func First[C Container](c C) (C.Element, bool) {
	return c.At(0)
}
```

Go retains implicit interface implementation. The compiler infers `Element` from method signatures. Generic code projects it as `C.Element`; the qualified form `Container.Element[C]` resolves ambiguity.

Associated types may be bound by name:

```go
var c Container[Element = string]
```

An interface with unbound associations is constraint-only. A fully bound interface may also be used as an ordinary interface value. The initial design excludes explicit `impl` declarations, hidden existential associations, generic associated types, defaults, and associated constants.

## Motivation

Go can already model a related type as an ordinary type parameter:

```go
type Container[E any] interface {
	Add(E)
	At(int) (E, bool)
}

func First[E any, C Container[E]](c C) (E, bool)
```

This works, but repeated parameters are only the visible symptom. Associated types address four deeper problems:

* **Type ownership.** `Element` is selected by a container implementation; `Node` and `Edge` by a graph. Treating them as independent parameters hides this functional dependency and permits APIs to appear more configurable than they are.
* **Invalid combinations.** Separate parameters do not directly state that a cache and loader must use the same key/value pair. A binding such as `Loader[Key = C.Key, Value = C.Value]` makes that invariant part of the constraint and rejects mismatches during interface satisfaction.
* **Implementation-dependent results.** An operation can return `D.Value` or `P.AST`, with the result type determined by a decoder or parser, without exposing another caller-selected parameter in every API.
* **Composition and abstraction boundaries.** Middleware can preserve the request/response types of the service it wraps. At a runtime boundary, `Repository[ID = UserID, Entity = User]` permits dynamic implementations while retaining the complete static relationship.

Ordinary type parameters are selected at generic instantiation; associated types are determined by an interface implementation. The goal is therefore not merely shorter signatures, but declaring and enforcing a stable type relationship once across algorithms, adapters, and interface values.

This feature is aimed at method-based abstractions. It does not improve APIs such as `slices.Clone[S ~[]E, E any]`: a slice has no methods from which to infer `E`, and its representation is intentionally caller-selected.

## Proposal

### Declaration and projection

A non-parameterized named interface may declare associated types:

```go
type Graph interface {
	type Node comparable
	type Edge any

	Nodes() []Node
	EdgesFrom(Node) []Edge
	Endpoints(Edge) (Node, Node)
}
```

The declaration form is `type Name Constraint`. The name is in scope throughout the interface, and its constraint has the same meaning as a type parameter constraint.

For a type parameter `T`, an association is normally projected as `T.A`:

```go
type NodeSet[G Graph] map[G.Node]struct{}
```

This short form is valid when `T`'s constraint exposes exactly one association named `A`. Otherwise the origin-qualified form is required:

```go
Graph.Node[G]
graph.Graph.Node[G]
```

The qualified form is also required for a concrete implementing type, whose method set alone does not identify which structural interface owns `A`.

An association's identity is its declaring interface plus its name. Embedding the same origin through several paths produces one association; same-named associations from different origins remain distinct. Therefore `T.Element` is ambiguous when `T` embeds unrelated `Source.Element` and `Destination.Element`, but both qualified projections remain valid.

Every association must occur in at least one method parameter or result where structural type matching can determine it. Declarations without such an occurrence are invalid. Every implementation must produce one unique witness; associations requiring an explicit witness are outside this proposal.

### Binding

Associations are bound by name after the interface:

```go
Container[Element = string]
Graph[Node = string, Edge = int64]
```

Binding order is insignificant. Each name must identify an association and its right-hand type must satisfy the declared constraint. A binding may use a type parameter or another projection:

```go
func Copy[
	S Source,
	D Destination[Element = S.Element],
](src S, dst D) error
```

When embedded origins reuse a name, bindings must be qualified:

```go
Combined[Source.Element = T, Destination.Element = T]
```

The two associations are not merged; assigning both to `T` explicitly states their equality.

Bindings narrow the interface type set; they do not create new defined types. Partial binding is allowed in constraints. Positional binding such as `Graph[string, int64]` is not part of this design.

### Interface values

An interface with an unbound association may be used only as a constraint:

```go
var c Container // invalid: Element is unknown

func Size[C Container](c C) int // valid constraint use
```

A fully bound interface has a complete method set and may be a value type:

```go
var c Container[Element = string] = new(Slice[string])
value, ok := c.At(0) // value has type string
```

After substitution, this interface has ordinary methods such as `Add(string)` and `At(int) (string, bool)`. It therefore uses the existing interface value and dispatch representation; no runtime witness table is added.

The type set of `I[A = X]` contains the types that implement `I` with witness `A` identical to `X`. Its identity consists of `I` and its normalized, order-independent binding map. It is not identical to an equivalent interface literal, although the two are mutually assignable when their normalized type sets agree. Two bound uses of the same origin are identical exactly when every binding is identical. A fully bound associated interface is basic when its normalized form contains only methods and embedded basic interfaces; it may then appear in type assertions and type switches under existing rules.

A partially bound interface remains constraint-only:

```go
func Visit[G Graph[Node = string]](g G) {} // valid
var g Graph[Node = string]                 // invalid: Edge is unbound
```

Allowing plain `var g Graph` would hide both the implementation and the types needed to call its methods. Supporting that requires existential types, which are outside this proposal.

### Implicit implementation

Implementation remains structural. Associated witnesses are inferred by matching methods:

```go
type Slice[E any] []E

func (s *Slice[E]) Add(v E) { *s = append(*s, v) }
func (s *Slice[E]) At(i int) (E, bool) {
	if i < 0 || i >= len(*s) {
		var zero E
		return zero, false
	}
	return (*s)[i], true
}
```

Comparing `*Slice[E]` with `Container` uniquely establishes:

```text
Container.Element[*Slice[E]] = E
```

No declaration is required on `Slice`, preserving Go's implicit satisfaction model.

### Type checking and inference

To check whether `T` implements an associated interface `I`, the type checker:

1. creates a variable for every unbound association;
2. applies explicit bindings as equality equations;
3. substitutes the variables into `I`'s method signatures;
4. matches those signatures against `T`'s method set;
5. solves a unique witness for every variable; and
6. checks each witness against its constraint.

Matching is first-order structural unification. It decomposes identical Go type constructors such as pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, and generic instantiations. It does not enumerate union alternatives, search for an implementing type, or backtrack among witnesses. Satisfaction fails if a witness is absent, non-unique, inconsistent, cyclic, or outside its constraint. For example, `Put(Item)` and `Get() Item` cannot match `Put(string)` and `Get() int`.

Projection inference is deliberately one-way: after `T` is known, `T.A` can be normalized; `T` is not inferred from `T.A` alone.

```go
func AppendOne[C Container](c C, v C.Element) { c.Add(v) }

var s Slice[string]
AppendOne(&s, "hello") // C is inferred first; C.Element becomes string
```

Conversely, `NewValue[C Container](v C.Element) C` cannot infer `C` from the argument alone. This restriction avoids reverse or higher-order search.

### Grammar sketch

```ebnf
AssociatedTypeDecl = "type" identifier TypeConstraint .
AssociatedBinding  = AssociatedName "=" Type .
AssociatedName     = [ TypeName "." ] identifier .
ShortProjection    = TypeParamName "." identifier .
QualifiedProjection = TypeName "." identifier TypeArgs .
```

`=` distinguishes a binding list from ordinary generic instantiation. Because the initial design permits associations only in non-parameterized interfaces, ordinary arguments and associated bindings cannot be mixed.

## Representative examples

### Graph algorithm families

Graph algorithms need node and edge types only because they belong to `G`. Today every algorithm must propagate both:

```go
func BFS[N comparable, E any, G Graph[N, E]](
	g G, start N, visit func(N) bool,
) error

func TopologicalSort[N comparable, E any, G Graph[N, E]](
	g G,
) ([]N, error)

func TransitiveReduction[N comparable, E any, G Graph[N, E]](
	g G,
) (G, error)
```

With associations, the same family quantifies only over `G`:

```go
func BFS[G Graph](
	g G, start G.Node, visit func(G.Node) bool,
) error

func TopologicalSort[G Graph](g G) ([]G.Node, error)
func TransitiveReduction[G Graph](g G) (G, error)
```

The benefit compounds across the package. Adding `Weight` also does not force algorithms that never name it to propagate another parameter.

### Service middleware stacks (Tower)

Rust Tower builds clients and servers by stacking middleware over `Service<Request>`. Each layer preserves types selected by the wrapped service.

Ordinary Go generics repeat request and response types at every layer:

```go
type Timeout[Req, Resp any, S Service[Req, Resp]] struct{ inner S }
type Retry[Req, Resp any, S Service[Req, Resp]] struct{ inner S }

var h *Retry[Request, Response,
	*Timeout[Request, Response, *Backend],
]
```

A Go-shaped associated interface carries the relationship once:

```go
type Service interface {
	type Request any
	type Response any

	Ready(context.Context) error
	Call(context.Context, Request) (Response, error)
}

type Timeout[S Service] struct{ inner S }
type Retry[S Service] struct{ inner S }

// Retry forwarding methods use S.Request and S.Response; omitted.

var h *Retry[*Timeout[*Backend]]

func (t *Timeout[S]) Ready(ctx context.Context) error
func (t *Timeout[S]) Call(
	ctx context.Context, req S.Request,
) (S.Response, error)
```

Timeout, retry, tracing, rate limiting, and load balancing then carry only `S`.

Tower's exact Rust trait makes `Request` a parameter and `Response`, `Error`, and `Future` associations. A literal port needs parameterized associated interfaces and deeper `Future` inference, both excluded here.

### Cache composition and type equality

A cache fixes a key/value pair. TTL, metrics, tracing, sharding, and single-flight wrappers must preserve that pair. With ordinary parameters:

```go
type TTL[K comparable, V any, C Cache[K, V]] struct{ inner C }
type Metrics[K comparable, V any, C Cache[K, V]] struct{ inner C }

var old *Metrics[UserID, User,
	*TTL[UserID, User, *RedisUserCache],
]
```

With associations, every wrapper carries only the cache:

```go
type Cache interface {
	type Key comparable
	type Value any

	Get(context.Context, Key) (Value, bool, error)
	Set(context.Context, Key, Value, time.Duration) error
}

type TTL[C Cache] struct{ inner C }
type Metrics[C Cache] struct{ inner C }

// Forwarding methods use C.Key and C.Value; omitted.

var current *Metrics[*TTL[*RedisUserCache]]
```

`RedisUserCache` therefore fixes the key/value pair for the whole stack.

Associations also express equality between separate abstractions. A cache-aside loader must produce exactly the cache's key and value types:

```go
type Loader interface {
	type Key comparable
	type Value any
	Load(context.Context, Key) (Value, error)
}

func ReadThrough[
	C Cache,
	L Loader[Key = C.Key, Value = C.Value],
](ctx context.Context, c C, l L, key C.Key) (C.Value, error)
```

The current form needs four parameters—`K`, `V`, `C Cache[K, V]`, and `L Loader[K, V]`. The associated form names the real participants, `C` and `L`, and rejects a mismatched loader at compile time.

### Repository runtime boundaries

Repositories demonstrate the separate benefit of fully bound interface values:

```go
type Repository interface {
	type ID comparable
	type Entity any

	Find(context.Context, ID) (Entity, bool, error)
	Save(context.Context, Entity) error
}

type UserService struct {
	repo Repository[ID = UserID, Entity = User]
}

func NewUserService(
	repo Repository[ID = UserID, Entity = User],
) *UserService
```

The service accepts SQL, in-memory, or decorated implementations through normal dispatch while guaranteeing the same `UserID`/`User` pair.

## Design rationale and limits

Witness inference preserves structural interfaces. Rust-style explicit `impl` declarations would introduce coherence, ownership, and cross-package conflict rules that Go does not otherwise need.

The short projection `T.A` keeps common generic code readable. The qualified form `I.A[T]` handles unrelated structural interfaces that reuse the same name.

Requiring complete binding for interface values avoids existential types while still supporting fields, return values, dependency injection, and collections whose elements agree on every association.

The cost is additional parser, type-checker, tooling, and language complexity. The initial design limits that cost by excluding explicit witnesses, hidden associations, generic associated types, defaults, reverse inference, and associations on parameterized or anonymous interfaces.

## Comparison with other languages

### Rust

Rust traits declare associated types and select them in an `impl`:

```rust
trait Iterator {
    type Item;
    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>;
}
```

Rust projects `<T as Iterator>::Item` and binds trait objects with syntax such as `dyn Graph<Node = String>`. Go instead infers witnesses from structural methods, normally projects `T.Item`, and permits interface values only after all associations are bound.

### Swift

Swift protocols use `associatedtype`, infer witnesses from conformances, and express equality with `where` clauses such as `C1.Item == C2.Item`. The proposed Go design is similar, but Go's structural interfaces require an optional origin-qualified projection to resolve same-named associations.

## Alternatives

### Ordinary type parameters

The status quo is simpler and remains preferable for caller-selected types. Its weakness is repeated propagation when one type determines the others.

### Binding syntax

This proposal uses named inline bindings:

```go
Graph[Node = string, Edge = int64]
```

It is concise, order-independent, and supports partial binding. Three other forms were considered:

```go
// Interface-body binding: Go-like composition, but verbose at use sites.
type StringGraph interface {
	Graph
	type Node = string
	type Edge = int64
}

// Generic adapter: conventional use, but requires an extra declaration.
type GraphOf[N comparable, E any] interface {
	Graph
	type Node = N
	type Edge = E
}
var g GraphOf[string, int64]

// Positional binding: short, but ambiguous with generic instantiation.
var g Graph[string, int64]

// Where binding: explicit, but starts a broader constraint language.
var g Graph where Node = string, Edge = int64
```

The most conservative alternative is to make interface-body binding the only primitive and use `GraphOf` adapters by convention. The witness and interface value semantics are unchanged by this syntax choice.

### Other mechanisms

Marker methods expose types indirectly but pollute method sets and still need ordinary parameters. Explicit `impl` declarations violate implicit satisfaction. General type functions or `where` clauses are more powerful and require substantially broader inference rules. Always requiring `I.A[T]` is unambiguous but makes common signatures needlessly long.

## Compatibility

The proposal is source-compatible with existing valid Go. These forms are invalid today: `type` declarations in interfaces, `T.A` as a type projection, `I.A[T]` where `I` is a type, and `=` inside type argument lists. Existing interfaces and implementation relationships are unchanged. Source using the feature would require an appropriate Go language version.

Changing a method that determines an association, adding a conflicting method, or tightening an association constraint can change interface satisfaction and is therefore a breaking API change.

Fully bound interfaces normalize to ordinary method sets before runtime metadata is emitted. Reflection sees those normalized methods; this proposal adds no runtime API for associations or witnesses.

## Implementation impact

The parser, AST, formatter, and printer must represent declarations, bindings, and projections. `go/types` and the compiler need dependent projections, witness maps, first-order unification, cycle detection, and caching by interface/type pair. Export data must preserve association origins.

Function inference gains projection-normalization work items, but no reverse or higher-order solving. Checks perform no global search or witness backtracking; apart from existing constraint checks, work is bounded by the compared method signatures and cached per pair. Fully bound interfaces continue to use existing itabs and the two-word interface representation. `gopls`, documentation, analyzers, and code generators must understand the new forms.

Acceptance should require a prototype that:

* checks concrete and generic witnesses, bindings, embedding, and conflicts;
* verifies ordinary dispatch for fully bound interface values;
* translates real graph, service, cache, and repository APIs, recording propagated parameters and wrapper-instantiation size;
* compares diagnostics and maintenance changes with ordinary generics; and
* measures compiler and `go/types` cost on feature and control corpora.

The proposal should advance only if that prototype shows a material API benefit without a material regression for code that does not use associated types.

## Open issues

* Should binding use inline named syntax or interface-body bindings plus optional generic adapters?
* Should a future proposal support associations on parameterized interfaces, motivated by Tower's `Service<Request>` split?
* Are explicit witnesses or hidden existential associations ever justified?
* Should reflection eventually expose association declarations?

No prototype or target Go release is proposed yet.

items.body:
### Proposal Details

Every so often, I find myself writing simple wrappers for `io.Reader`. My user-facing function returns an `io.Reader`, but secretly it wants to process reads as well. This can be to implement things like progress bars, metrics, or hashing.

```
Underlying reader -> my function -> developer consumer
```

The way to do this currently is to create a struct type that fulfills the `io.Reader` interface, wrap the underlying reader in that struct, and then return my reader. This is verbose and takes me out of the function I'm currently writing. It would be cleaner if the `io` package could do this for me, and I just pass in my implementation of `Read`. This is similar to `http.HandleFunc`.

```go
func WrapReader(r io.Reader, f func([]byte) (int, error)) *io.ReaderWrapper
func WrapWriter(w io.Writer, f func([]byte) (int, error)) *io.WriterWrapper
```

One thing I'm not sure about is how to handle different interfaces, for example also supporting `io.ReadCloser`. The naive option is to just add different function wrappers for each of those, but ideally you wouldn't have to, and calls to `Close` would just pass through to the underlying interface if it supports it. Maybe the `io` struct for this would just fulfill all the interfaces and do checks in each of them?

Probably these middleware functions should be allowed to modify the data before it gets passed on, to allow different use cases.

Overall, I see this proposal as a way to improve Go ergonomics and prevent repetition, similar to other helper functions like `io.ReadFull`. Thanks!

items.title: proposal: crypto/x509: remove x509sha1 GODEBUG in Go 1.24
items.body:
Go 1.18 disabled the use of SHA1 in most X.509 certificates by default but added a GODEBUG for re-enabling them, to accommodate private CAs that might not have updated yet. <https://go.dev/crypto/x509#InsecureAlgorithmError>

Per <https://go.dev/doc/godebug#go-118> we can remove that GODEBUG in Go 1.22 or later. The GKE team, which is the only team that reached out about needing to keep SHA1, has gathered metrics about their own dependence (via customers) on this setting, and they believe that they won't need it anymore after Go 1.23. 

Unless there are other users who need us to keep the setting around longer, I propose that we retire the x509sha1 GODEBUG in Go 1.24. We would pre-announce this in the release notes for both Go 1.22 and Go 1.23.

items.title: proposal: Parameter-level `noescape` modifier for function types

milestone.title: Proposal
milestone.description:
Proposals that are pending (not yet accepted/rejected).
See https://go.dev/s/proposal-process.

items.body:
### Proposal Details

# Proposal: Parameter-level `noescape` modifier for function types

## Summary

Add a `noescape` parameter modifier to Go function parameter declarations and function types that tells the compiler the parameter will not escape the callee or any synchronous callees.

Example:

```go
type Handler func(noescape buf []byte)

func Call(h Handler, data []byte) {
    // Call may pass a stack-backed slice to h and the compiler will know h
    // (and functions it calls synchronously) will not cause `data` to be
    // moved to the heap.
    h(data)
}
```

This extends the existing `//go:noescape` directive (today only usable on external/assembly-defined functions) into ordinary Go function types.

## Motivation

Escape analysis often forces arguments onto the heap if the compiler cannot prove they don’t escape. Programmers often know an argument is only used synchronously, but:

* Must use `//go:noescape` with assembly stubs, or
* Pay for heap allocations, or
* Resort to `unsafe`.

A `noescape` modifier on parameters expresses that guarantee in the type system. This unlocks stack allocation, avoids heap moves, and enables high-performance callback APIs without unsafe tricks.

The Go repo already uses a directive `//go:noescape` to promise non-escaping behavior for external/assembly-declared functions; however that pragma is limited in applicability. A language-level `noescape` modifier makes the promise usable on ordinary function values and types.

## Proposal

### Syntax

Extend parameter declarations with an optional `noescape` modifier:

```go
func Do(f func(noescape b []byte))

type Handler func(noescape buf []byte)

var h = func(noescape b []byte) { /* ... */ }
```

Multiple parameters may be marked:

```go
func Two(a int, noescape b []byte, noescape c []byte)
```

### Semantics

* `noescape` promises the parameter will not outlive the current call stack frame.
* The callee must not:
  * Store the parameter into heap/global memory.
  * Capture it in a goroutine.
  * Return it.
  * Assign it to variables with longer lifetimes.
* The compiler enforces this at compile time.
* Type system:
  * `func(noescape T)` is distinct from `func(T)`.
  * `func(noescape T)` can be assigned to `func(T)`, but not vice versa.

### Implications
 * The compiler must halt as soon as the user tries to assign a function to that type where the implementation violates the noescape property of this parameter (this is checked in escape analysis)

### Errors

Any use that violates the promise is a compile-time error, e.g. capturing in a goroutine.

## Examples

**Valid:**

```go
type Writer func(noescape buf []byte)

func Use(w Writer) {
    b := make([]byte, 128) // stays on stack
    w(b)
}

func Good(noescape buf []byte) {
    _ = len(buf)
}
```

**Invalid:**

```go
func Bad(noescape buf []byte) {
    go func() {
        // ERROR: capturing noescape buf in goroutine
        _ = buf[0]
    }()
}
```

## Implementation

* **Parser/Type checker:** allow `noescape` keyword on params, enforce type/assignment rules.
* **Escape analysis:** propagate the promise across synchronous calls.
* **SSA/Codegen:** keep eligible args stack-allocated.
* **Tooling:** vet / `-m` should report violations and optimizations.

## Compatibility

* 100% backward compatible — old code compiles unchanged.
* Only new code using `noescape` will be rejected if it breaks the rules.
* Existing `//go:noescape` pragmas remain supported.

## Alternatives

* Stick with `//go:noescape` + assembly stubs.
* Add `unsafe` intrinsics.
* Rely on escape analysis improvements only.

## Non-goals

* Returning stack pointers.
* Storing `noescape` values into heap data.
* Changing GC semantics.

## Migration / Use cases

* I/O libraries that want callbacks with stack-backed buffers.
* Cryptographic APIs to avoid heap allocation of sensitive buffers.
* Libraries currently using `//go:noescape` assembly stubs.

## Implementation Plan

1. Parser/type-checker prototype.
2. Escape analysis integration.
3. SSA/codegen optimizations.
4. Documentation, vet integration, benchmarks.

## Open Questions

* Should it ever apply to return values? (Probably not.)
* How best to handle cross-package diagnostics?
* Exact variance rules for type conversion.

## Rationale

* Brings `//go:noescape` into the type system.
* Gives programmers safe, explicit control.
* Strong compile-time checks prevent misuse.

## Related Work

* Go’s existing `//go:noescape` pragma (for assembly stubs).
* Swift had `@noescape` for closures.
* Other languages/libraries use similar concepts for lifetimes.

items.title: proposal: testing: allow settings flags for the duration of a test

milestone.title: Proposal
milestone.description:
Proposals that are pending (not yet accepted/rejected).
See https://go.dev/s/proposal-process.

items.body:
### Proposal Details

When tests require a certain flag value to work, `flag.Set(...)` is often chosen as the go-to way.
An example:

```go
import "testing"

func TestSomeFeature(t *testing.T) {
    err := flag.Set("enable_some_feature", "true")
    if err != nil {
        t.Fatal(err)
    }
    // Trigger the feature and make assertions.
}
```

There are some downsides to this approach, most importantly these:
1. Parallel tests may encounter race conditions and panic when calling the `flag.Set` function.
2. The flag value is set throughout the test process, i.e. affects other tests are well, while it shouldn't.

I propose having a `func (t* testing.T) SetFlag(name, value string)` function that makes the flag set goroutine-safe and only affect a single test scope, i.e. the flag is reset to default value when `t` is done.

items.body:
### Proposal Details

# Proposal: Allow declaring functions with `defer` directly

## Background

Currently in Go, `defer` can only be used inside the body of a function,
to schedule cleanup or finalization code to run before the function returns.

For example:

```go
func Example() {
    defer func() {
        cleanup()
    }()
    // rest of code
}
```

This is sometimes verbose when the entire function is conceptually a
“deferred scope”. The developer intent is to say: *“this function is just
a defer with logic inside”*.

## Proposal

Allow declaring a function as a deferred function directly:

```go
defer func Example() {
    cleanup()
    // rest of code
}
```

This is equivalent to today’s syntax:

```go
func Example() {
    defer func() {
        cleanup()
    }()
}
```

The new form removes one nested `func(){}` wrapper and makes intent more
explicit: the whole function body is a deferred scope.

## Rationale

- Improves readability for functions whose sole purpose is running deferred
  logic (setup + cleanup).
- Reduces boilerplate by avoiding an extra anonymous function.
- Makes intent clearer when the main body of a function is essentially a
  resource scope.

## Compatibility

This change is backward compatible: existing code continues to work.

The proposal only introduces new syntax for a case that is already valid
with more boilerplate today.

## Alternatives considered

- Keep status quo: write `defer func(){ ... }()`.  
- Use helper functions or code generation to wrap deferred scopes.  
- These alternatives work, but they do not improve readability at the
  language level.

## Conclusion

Allowing `defer func Name(){ ... }` provides a more concise and expressive
way to declare functions that are meant to act as deferred scopes.

items.body:
Currently, the `http.Transport` implementation will reuse an HTTP connection if keepalives are enabled and the connection has not been in an idle state for too long.
This means that for high throughput connections that are always active and rarely/never exceed the `IdleConnTimeout` limit, the connection will keep getting reused (as long as it is not broken).

This poses a problem in terms of service discovery and client-side load balancing - since address resolution only happens in the dialer's `DialContext`, this leaves no chance for the client to re-resolve the target address since the same connection is constantly reused without ever "re-dialing".

I propose to add a `MaxConnectionAge` flag to `http.Transport` that would limit the lifetime of a persistent connection, and would not reuse it beyond this lifetime.

This would be in line with the behavior of `go-grpc` which [also enforces a `MaxConnectionAge` limit](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-go/issues/3170).

### Proposal Details

`iter.Seq` and `iter.Seq2` open a wide range of possibilities to provide iterable views of data structures without involving memory copies.

While the Go standard library already provides some helper functions to create `iter.Seq` (e.g. `slices.Values`) or `iter.Seq2` (e.g. `maps.All`), it still lacks many usual functions to manipulate the sequences (e.g. filtering, modifying) or aggregating them (e.g. `Reduce`, `Max`, `Min`).

I would like to offer the `iters` package to fill this gap: https://github.com/mariomac/iters , the donation would contain whole package, or just a part, depending on the Go community needs and criteria.

`iters` is a simple package relying only on the Go standard library that provides the following group of functionalities:
* Instantiation of sequences (`instantiate.go`): creates sequences from slices, maps, varargs, numeric ranges, channels, and other sequences. It also allows generating infinite sequences from generator functions, or concatenating sequences.
* Transformations of sequences (`transformers.go`): modify sequences (`Map`, `Peek`), filter them (`Filter`, `Distinct`), cut them (`Limit`, `Skip`)...
* Aggregations of sequences (`terminals.go`):  functional `Reduce` operator, common aggregators like `Count`, `Max`, `Min`, booleans (`AllMatch`, `AnyMatch`, `NoneMatch`), etc...

Some examples in the project README: https://github.com/mariomac/iters/blob/main/README.md

For more information about the provided functions, please go to the API documentation https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/mariomac/iters

Key points of the `iters` package:
* Convenience methods for common operations, based on a well-known specification like the Java Streams API, for faster familiarization with developers.
* Lazy evaluation allows working with infinite sequences without involving any copy of memory.
